title: Database per Service Pattern
description: Learn the database per service pattern and why it is essential for microservices autonomy.

data.text: The database per service pattern gives each microservice its own private database, ensuring loose coupling and independent evolution. Amazon, Uber, and Netflix all use this pattern to allow teams to change their data models without coordinating with others.

Each microservice owns its database exclusively. No other service can access the database directly. Services communicate only through APIs, which enforces encapsulation and allows each team to choose the right database technology for their needs.

data.title: Database per Service Trade-offs
items: Autonomy: Teams can evolve their schema independently
Technology diversity: Use PostgreSQL for orders, MongoDB for logs, Redis for cache
Scalability: Scale databases independently based on service needs
Decentralized data management: Each team owns its data
Challenge: Cross-service queries require APIs, not SQL joins

data.title: Polyglot Persistence
data.text: Database per service enables polyglot persistence: using the right database for each service. Amazon uses DynamoDB for high-throughput services and Aurora for transactional services.

data.title: Example: Database Assignment by Service
data.code:
# User Service -> PostgreSQL (relational, ACID)
# Product Catalog Service -> Elasticsearch (search-optimized)
# Recommendation Service -> Neo4j (graph database)
# Analytics Service -> BigQuery (data warehouse)
# Session Service -> Redis (in-memory key-value)

# Each service connects only to its own database:
# user-service -> postgresql://user-db:5432
# product-service -> elasticsearch://product-db:9200
# recommendation-service -> neo4j://rec-db:7687

items.question: Is database per service always best?
items.answer: For autonomous teams and complex domains, yes. For small teams or simple domains, a shared database may be acceptable as a starting point.

items.question: What about transactions across services?
items.answer: You cannot use distributed transactions with database per service. Use Saga pattern or eventual consistency instead.

items.question: How do I query across services?
items.answer: Use APIs, materialized views, or CQRS with dedicated read models. Direct SQL joins across services are not possible.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Each service owns its database exclusively
Enables polyglot persistence and team autonomy
Requires new patterns for cross-service data access
data.takeaway: Database per service is the foundation of autonomous microservices; avoid shared databases whenever possible.
